segments.input: How much noise does it take to make entropy behave? An Evidence Press briefing. Take two independent copies of a random signal, add Gaussian noise to each, and blend the two noisy copies, with a mixing weight that runs from all of one copy to an even blend. Mixing tends to make things more Gaussian, and Gaussians have the most entropy, so a natural guess is that entropy rises smoothly as you blend, with no dips: in mathematical terms, that it is a concave function of the mixing weight. Ball, Nayar and Tkocz conjectured exactly this. This year Luo disproved it, and showed that tiny symmetric bumps on a Gaussian signal can still create a dip at an even blend whenever the signal makes up more than four sevenths of the total variance. Below one half, a positive result was already known.

segments.input: The question was what happens in between. This paper answers it. For any signal fraction below four sevenths, every symmetric signal close enough to a Gaussian gives a concave entropy curve. In noise terms: concavity is guaranteed once the noise variance exceeds three quarters of the signal variance, a signal-to-noise ratio of four thirds. Above that level the paper sharpens the counterexamples, with an exact formula for the dip's curvature. Part of that sign was proposed shortly before, in a public online argument, which the paper cites. It also explains where four sevenths comes from: the fixed point of a sharp Gaussian smoothing inequality. Two cautions. These are local results, and the effects are minute, dips of around ten to the minus thirteen in entropy.

segments.input: And whether exactly four sevenths itself qualifies is still open. The proofs are written out, and checked by standard-library scripts that must catch sixteen deliberately broken copies. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, published on the third of November twenty twenty-six; its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page.
